name: The Lucas Critique
statement: You cannot predict a policy's effects from past patterns, because people change their behaviour when policy changes.
statementAccent: people change their behaviour when policy changes
meaning: It is naive to forecast the effects of a new economic policy purely from the statistical relationships seen in past data, because those relationships are not fixed. They shift when policy changes, since rational people revise their expectations and their decisions in response to the new regime. A correlation that held under the old policy need not survive the attempt to exploit it.
mechanism: The relationships an econometric model estimates (a Phillips curve linking inflation and unemployment, say) are built up from the optimising decisions of individuals, and those decisions depend on what policy people expect. Change the policy rule and you change the expectations baked into the relationships, so the estimated coefficients move. The critique distinguishes deep structural parameters (preferences, technology, constraints), which are assumed invariant to policy, from reduced-form relationships, which embed expectations and are not. Valid policy evaluation must model the deep parameters and expectations explicitly.

examples.text: The historical inflation-unemployment trade-off looked exploitable in mid-century data, but when authorities tried to buy lower unemployment with higher inflation, expectations adjusted and the trade-off broke down: the stagflation of the 1970s, the paradigm case.

Observing no robberies while guards stand watch does not mean the guards can safely be removed — removing them changes the incentives of would-be robbers, just as a policy change alters the behaviour behind an observed relationship.
Lucas showed the estimated slope of a Phillips curve can depend on how variable monetary policy has been, so the relationship itself shifts whenever the monetary regime shifts.

variants.name: Rational expectations
variants.text: The hypothesis at the critique's core: that people form expectations efficiently, consistent with the actual structure of the economy, and so respond to the policy rule itself.

variants.name: Microfoundations and DSGE
variants.text: The methodological response: building macro models up from deep parameters of household and firm behaviour, so they aim to survive policy changes rather than break under them.

whyItMatters: It reshaped macroeconomics, driving the field toward microfounded models built on deep parameters and expectations, and remains a permanent caution against reading past correlations as stable policy levers. Lucas won the 1995 Nobel for developing and applying rational expectations, which this critique put at the centre of the discipline.

working.lead: Distrust historical correlations under new policy
working.text: before predicting a policy's effect, ask whether the relationship you are relying on would itself shift once the policy changes.
base policy evaluation on preferences, technology, and constraints, which are more likely invariant, rather than on reduced-form coefficients.
treat how people anticipate and respond to the policy rule as part of the analysis, not a fixed background.

limits: The critique is a methodological argument, not an empirical law, and its practical magnitude is contested. Several studies find that reduced-form relationships often do not show the parameter instability the critique predicts across documented policy shifts, treating it as a testable hypothesis with mixed support. The counter-evidence runs both ways. Even the microfounded models built to be critique-proof have been found to have unstable deep parameters, raising doubt about whether truly policy-invariant parameters exist. Its core logic is widely accepted; how much it matters in practice is not settled.
misreadings: It does not say forecasting is impossible or that all econometrics is worthless, only that relationships estimated under one policy regime cannot be assumed to hold when the regime changes. And it is a specific claim about expectations shifting behaviour, not a vague warning that models are imperfect.
origin: Made by the economist Robert Lucas in 'Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique,' Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy, vol. 1, pp. 19-46 (1976); Lucas received the 1995 Nobel Memorial Prize for the rational-expectations programme it advanced.
